analysis.one_liner: Bars new mining on about 234,000 acres of federal land beside the Boundary Waters in Minnesota.
analysis.headline: The House Natural Resources Committee approved the bill on a 24–16 vote and reported it to the full House in December 2022, but no floor vote was ever held before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently withdraw about 234,328 acres of federal land and water in Minnesota's Rainy River Watershed from new mining claims, mineral leasing, and related activity, making it off-limits to new copper-nickel and other hardrock mines [S2] [S4]. The area sits next to the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, and water in the watershed drains through it, so a mine spill there could foul one of the country's most visited wilderness areas [S2]. The bill does leave one carve-out: the Forest Service could still allow removal of sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite from lands in the area if it finds the removal would not harm water, air, or forest habitat [S2] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Minnesotans and visitors who use the Boundary Waters and Voyageurs National Park, businesses in towns like Ely that sell canoe trips, lodging, and supplies to wilderness travelers, and anyone downstream who relies on clean water in a watershed that drains toward Lake Superior.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Boundary Waters visitors and wilderness tourism towns

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws about 234,328 acres of federal land and water in the Rainy River Watershed from new mining claims, entry, disposal, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing, closing the area to new hardrock mining

Protects land adjacent to the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, where sulfide-ore copper mining poses a long-term pollution risk to the watershed that flows into the wilderness and toward Lake Superior
Makes the protection automatic for any land in the area the United States later acquires, so the ban cannot be quietly eroded through land deals

Preserves existing local uses: the Forest Service may still permit removal of sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite inside the area as long as it would not damage water, air, or forest habitat

analysis.who_pays: Copper-nickel mining companies holding mineral rights or leases in the watershed — most prominently the company seeking to build a large copper-nickel mine there — and the mining jobs those projects would have created in northeastern Minnesota. The country also forgoes some domestic supply of copper and nickel, minerals used in batteries and electric vehicles, though those can be mined elsewhere.
analysis.who_pays_short: Copper-nickel mining companies and mine jobs

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal permanently closes a mineral-rich area to new mining, foreclosing any new mining jobs and royalty revenue from that specific land

The bill removes land from copper and nickel production even as the country looks for domestic sources of battery minerals; critics argue modern mining with safeguards can coexist with wilderness, and the bill does not put that argument to a site-specific test
The protection depends on an act of Congress and could be repealed by a future Congress, so it is a political shield rather than a physical one

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a permanent, certain loss of new mining potential on one tract of federal land for permanent protection of a watershed that feeds a nationally significant wilderness and a large existing tourism economy. The cost falls on a concentrated group — mining companies and prospective mine workers — while the benefit is diffuse and long-lasting: clean water and an intact wilderness. The carve-out for iron ore, taconite, granite, sand, and gravel softens the economic hit without touching the main risk, sulfide-ore copper mining.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee approved and reported the bill to the full House in mid-December 2022, but House leaders never brought it to the floor for a vote before the session ended two weeks later.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in April 2021 and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, which sent it to two subcommittees covering parks and mineral resources
The subcommittees held a hearing in May 2022, then were discharged so the full committee could take the bill up
On July 13, 2022, the committee ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 24 to 16
The committee formally reported the bill on December 14, 2022, and it was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills waiting for a full House vote
No further House action followed before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill never received an up-or-down vote in the House and had no Senate counterpart that advanced
All 58 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans signed on

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The copper-nickel mining companies with interests in the watershed are better off, because the land stayed open to mineral entry and the proposed mine's future was left to administrative decisions rather than a permanent congressional ban. The wilderness keeps today's existing protections but gained nothing new.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 58 cosponsors was a Democrat; the committee vote was 24–16, with the committee's Republicans supplying the no votes, and the bill never found a floor vote in a narrowly Democratic House.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently withdrawn the watershed from the mining laws, blocking new copper-nickel mines such as the one proposed there. Sulfide mining carries a risk of acid mine drainage that could pollute the Boundary Waters, whose appeal underpins a large outdoor-recreation economy — so the industry's gain would come at a lasting cost to the public's water and wilderness.

Outfitters, lodges, and guide businesses around the Boundary Waters depend on intact wilderness and clean water; a permanent mining ban protects the resource their livelihood rides on. Their interest runs directly with visitors and residents who want the water protected.

industries.industry: Iron ore, taconite, and aggregate producers
industries.note: The bill keeps a Forest Service permit pathway for removing iron ore, taconite, granite, sand, and gravel inside the area, so those existing uses are preserved even as new hardrock mining is barred.
